topics.title: When did my childhood go? Rationalism

learn.hook: Was there one day you stopped being a child? Markus Natten's poem keeps asking that question, and each answer is a step towards growing up.
points: 'Childhood' by Markus Natten reflects on the moment childhood is lost.
Four stanzas; the refrain 'When did my childhood go?' (a rhetorical question) structures the poem; each of the first three stanzas offers a possible answer.
Stanza 1 asks: was it the day he ceased to be eleven? Or the time he realised that Hell and Heaven could not be found in geography (on a map), and so could not exist?
This is rationalism: he began to think logically and to question beliefs that cannot be proved.
Rhetorical questions are asked for effect, not for an answer; repetition makes the search feel urgent.

example.q: What does the line about Hell and Heaven not being in geography suggest?
steps: Geography deals with real places on a map.
Hell and Heaven are not on any map.
So the child begins to reason that they may not be real: logical thinking.
example.answer: It marks the start of rational thinking: he questions ideas he cannot locate or prove.

learn.reallife: A Class 6 student who starts asking 'But how do we know?' about everything is showing the rationalism Natten describes. Science classes at school feed it.

topics.title: Hypocrisy and a mind of his own

learn.hook: Adults say 'share with others' and then fight over a parking spot. Spotting that gap is, says the poet, another sign that childhood is ending.
points: Stanza 2: perhaps childhood went when he saw that adults were not all they seemed to be.
They talked of love and preached of love, but did not act so lovingly: he recognised their hypocrisy.
Stanza 3: perhaps it went when he found his mind was really his own, to use whichever way he chose.
His thoughts were no longer borrowed from others but his own and his alone: individuality and independent thinking.
Stanza map: Stanza 1 – rationalism; Stanza 2 – hypocrisy of adults; Stanza 3 – individuality.

example.q: Identify the stanzas that deal with individuality, rationalism and hypocrisy.
steps: Stanza 1: Heaven and Hell not in geography – rationalism.
Stanza 2: adults preach love but don't act lovingly – hypocrisy.
Stanza 3: his mind is his own – individuality.
example.answer: Rationalism – Stanza 1; hypocrisy – Stanza 2; individuality – Stanza 3.

learn.reallife: Many Indian teens notice when elders say 'don't use phones at dinner' and then scroll themselves. Noticing that gap, and forming your own views, is part of growing up.

topics.title: Where did childhood go? Stanza 4 and devices

learn.hook: Look at a baby's face and you'll see it: total trust, total wonder. The poet says that's where his childhood went.
points: Stanza 4 changes the question from 'when' to 'where': where did my childhood go?
Answer: it went to some forgotten place hidden in an infant's face; that is all he knows.
Metaphor: childhood is a thing that has gone to a 'forgotten place'.
Nostalgia: childhood survives only in the innocence of an infant, which he can see but not regain.
Contrast between a child's and an adult's view; end rhyme in parts (e.g., eleven/Heaven, place/face). The poet's feeling: wistful longing for lost innocence.

example.q: What is the poet's feeling about childhood?
steps: He searches for the moment it was lost.
He accepts it is gone.
He sees it only in an infant's innocent face.
example.answer: He feels nostalgic and wistful; childhood is precious and lost, surviving only in a baby's innocence.

learn.reallife: Watch a toddler at a Diwali mela staring at lights with pure wonder. Adults can't get that back, which is exactly what Stanza 4 says.

topics.title: Growing up: themes and exam practice

learn.hook: Growing up isn't a birthday; it's a set of discoveries. The poem lists three, and exam questions love asking you to name them.
points: Main theme: loss of innocence and the process of growing up.
Growing up involves three stages: rationalism (logical questioning), recognising hypocrisy, and individuality (independent thought).
Growing up is gradual, not one fixed day; that is why the poet keeps asking 'when?'.
Most poetic lines (personal choice): many readers pick the infant's-face lines, because they turn a vague loss into a vivid, tender image.
Exam tips: extract MCQs on stages and devices; short answers (40–50 words) on what growing up involves.

example.q: What, according to the poem, does growing up involve?
steps: Questioning beliefs logically (rationalism).
Seeing that adults don't always practise what they preach (hypocrisy).
Learning to think for oneself (individuality).
example.answer: Growing up means learning to reason, recognising adult hypocrisy, and developing one's own mind.

learn.reallife: Psychologists describe adolescence as a time of questioning and forming identity: the same stages Natten lists in verse.
